blocks.text: The resignation of Deputy Governor of the Indonesian Bank of Great Juda on January 13, 2026 came at an unneutral time. It appears when the national economy is being sensitive, the market is easily agitated, and the state needs a calming signal. The changing of officials at the central bank, under these circumstances, has always been more than just the rotation of office. It reads as an attitude, even as a direction.

Therefore, when President Prabowo Subianto filed his own nephew's name, Thomas Djiwandono, as one of the future Deputy Governor of the BI, the issue immediately changed face. This is no longer just a matter of the administration or the complete absence of office. There's a symbolic layer too thick to ignore. The country is talking, whether it's aware or not.

Thomas Djiwandono is certainly not a figure without supplies. His foreign education is solid, his political experience is real, and his position as Vice Minister of Finance gives him direct access to fiscal policy retrieval. He also grew up in a family that was familiar with the monetary world. It's all a fact. But that's precisely why the question becomes sharper: why should it be him, and why now?

The Bank of Indonesia, since reform, has been treated with one primary concern: keeping distance from political power. It's not because the textile is always correct, but because the monetary stability is reliant on trust. Trust is not born of good will, but from a clear line. When that line starts to blur, the market usually reads faster than the state wants to admit.

The problem is, we're in an economic phase that doesn't give us space for symbolic mistakes. The Rupiah that touches the level of 17,000 per U.S. dollar is not just a number on the trade screen. It's an expression of tension. It reflects the accumulation of worries, both against global conditions and domestic policy directions. In situations like this, central banks are supposed to be anchors. Not a new source of question.

That pressure also comes from politics. The Prabowo government hasn't really achieved internal stability. Great policies launched in no time, from free diet to White Cooperative and Dantara, triggered an unfinished debate. The fat cabinet strengthens the impression that the state is moving heavily, expensive, and it's hard to simplify. Then there came the flood disaster in Sumatra, which once again opened up old wounds about the management of the environment and the ecological compromise that was repeated.

In a landscape like this, every Elite decision carries a double weight. The filing of Thomas Djiwandono to the Indonesian Bank does not stand alone. He met with public unrest, fiscally exhausted, and long-lasting suspicions of power and family relations. There's no law against causing problems. There's enough inappropriate taste.

Progrationally, everything looks neat. The president sends letters, the House does a test of feasibility, a working mechanism. But the Indonesian political experience taught us that crisis of trust is rarely born of a breach of procedure. It's grown from legitimate decisions, but it feels less like institutional ethics.

At this point, leadership is tested instead of courage taking steps, but by restraint. The Indonesian Bank is not a political experiment, let alone a symbol of family consolidation. It's an institution that works with trust as its key currency. When that belief is under attack, the impact doesn't just explode. It seeps, slowly, but deep.
